text.title: MCP Routing Failure Modes
text.summary: Six ways a live-sources layer becomes a standing tax, each with the observable symptom and the rule that prevents it.

failure.symptom: Nine servers connected. Sessions cost noticeably more than they did last quarter and short conversations are the worst affected proportionally.
failure.cause: Definitions are re-sent every request, so the charge is fixed per turn while the useful work is not. Nobody capped the set, and each individual addition was small.
failure.prevention: Declare a cap, measure the footprint of the routed set, and express the result in currency per session so it competes with other spending instead of hiding in a token count.

failure.symptom: A server is connected for a service whose CLI is already installed on the same machine, and the agent uses it for lookups the command answers in one call.
failure.cause: "Is there an MCP for this" was asked before "can the agent just run it", so a proportional cost was replaced with a fixed one.
failure.prevention: CLI is the default. Overriding it requires a written reason naming what the command structurally cannot do, and preferences do not qualify.

failure.symptom: The routing document says "better integration" and "more reliable" for four of six servers, and nobody can reconstruct what problem any of them solved.
failure.cause: The justification field was left open, so it collected the reasons people already had for what they had already installed.
failure.prevention: Four named justifications and nothing else. A source that fits none of them routes to CLI or to `neither`.

failure.symptom: The agent declines a task it should be able to do, or claims a capability is unavailable, while the server providing it is connected and healthy.
failure.cause: Deferred tool loading is on and the agent never fetched that definition, so the tool does not exist from its point of view. The symptom looks like a model failure rather than a wiring failure.
failure.prevention: If deferred loading is enabled, record the fallback: what the agent does on a miss, and how a miss is made visible rather than absorbed.

failure.symptom: A community-published server holds a token for a first-party service. It has full sight of every request and response it brokers, and nobody decided that.
failure.cause: Installation was treated as configuration rather than as widening the trust boundary, often because the server appeared in a catalogue.
failure.prevention: Credentials only to servers published by the owner of the data, through a scoped OAuth flow, with `first_party` and `credential_scope` recorded per source.

failure.symptom: A server works today, passes its own tests, and depends on Sampling or Roots. Nothing warns; the failure arrives on somebody else's schedule.
failure.cause: The implemented protocol revision was never recorded, so the 2026-07-28 move to stateless operation and its twelve-month deprecation clock started without an owner.
failure.prevention: Record `spec_revision` per source and a dated `migration_deadline` for anything earlier than 2026-07-28. A stateful justification against a stateless revision is a contradiction to resolve now, not later.
